overview: Three Department of State file-index sheets summarize diplomatic correspondence from roughly 1930 to 1934 concerning Japanese regulation of ship load lines. The papers trace efforts to continue the 1922 reciprocal arrangement under which Japan and the United States recognized one another’s load-line certificates while awaiting implementation of the International Load Line Convention of July 5, 1930; they also concern Japanese laws and regulations, recognition of certificates issued by Lloyd’s Register, the legal status of deck logs, an alleged violation of Japan’s Load Line Act, a British-Japanese agreement, and the possible authorization of timber load lines. The underlying telegrams, despatches, correspondence, and publications are described in the index but are not reproduced in the OCR supplied.

subfiles.title: List of Papers entries 13–14: provisional U.S.-Japanese load-line arrangement
subfiles.doc_type: list of papers / file index sheet
subfiles.about: An index sheet records the proposed continuation of reciprocal recognition of American and Japanese load-line certificates pending implementation of the 1930 convention.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reported on December 31, 1930, that Japan had agreed to recognize load-line certificates issued to American vessels pending new U.S. legislation and asked whether he might seek an extension of the arrangement until the convention of July 5, 1930, entered into force. The Department instructed him on January 14, 1931, to make the inquiry and obtain authoritative copies of Japanese load-line laws and rules. A March 30 despatch reported that Japan would provisionally extend the 1922 agreement if the United States reciprocally recognized Japanese certificates and enclosed the relevant Foreign Office correspondence and Japanese regulations.

subfiles.title: List of Papers entries 15–21: implementation, certificates, and logbooks
subfiles.doc_type: list of papers / file index sheet
subfiles.about: A continuation index summarizes interdepartmental and diplomatic papers on reciprocal certificate recognition, Japanese load-line enforcement, official logbooks, and related British and Lloyd’s documentation.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records 1931 consultations with the Department of Commerce that led the United States to approve continuation of the reciprocal arrangement and recognition of certificates issued by competent Japanese authorities. Later entries concern whether a deck log constituted the official logbook under Japanese law, certificates issued by the American Committee of Lloyd’s Register of Shipping, and correspondence over an alleged violation of Japan’s Load Line Act. It also cross-references a United Kingdom–Japan agreement signed in London on January 21, 1934, and notes that Japanese shipping-safety legislation resembling the International Load Line Convention was to take effect on March 1, 1934.

subfiles.title: List of Papers entry 22: Japanese ratification and timber load lines
subfiles.doc_type: list of papers / file index sheet
subfiles.about: An index entry notes a request to determine whether Japan had ratified the Load Line Convention or authorized timber load lines in its regulations.
subfiles.summary: The Department of Commerce requested an inquiry into Japan’s status under the Load Line Convention. It particularly sought confirmation of whether Japanese regulations permitted the inclusion of timber load lines. The entry is dated February 8, but the year is not legible or supplied in the OCR.

interest: The file is useful because it condenses the administrative history of a transitional maritime-safety regime: an older bilateral arrangement was maintained while the United States and Japan moved toward the standards of the 1930 international convention. It also reveals practical legal uncertainties—such as which shipboard record counted as the official log and whether timber load lines were authorized—that arose beneath high-level treaty policy. The references to Lloyd’s Register and the 1934 British-Japanese agreement permit comparison of American, British, and Japanese approaches to recognizing maritime certificates.
